title: “For a monk practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: he dwells often in disenchantment toward form,…
content: “For a monk practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: he dwells often in disenchantment toward form, toward feeling, toward perception, toward formations, toward consciousness. Dwelling often in disenchantment toward form … toward consciousness, he fully understands form … feeling … perception … formations … consciousness. By fully understanding them, he is freed from form, freed from feeling, freed from perception, freed from formations, freed from consciousness, freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

title: The feet are painted with lac and dye, The face is smeared with powder and paste — Enough to fool a fool, But not one…
content:
The feet are painted with lac and dye,
The face is smeared with powder and paste —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

title: “Monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the fool is generated. That ignorance the fool has not abandoned. That craving the…
content: “Monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the fool is generated. That ignorance the fool has not abandoned. That craving the fool has not destroyed. Why is that? Monks, the fool does not live the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, after death, the fool goes to another body. Having gone to another body, he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is not freed from suffering.”

title: “Rāhula, when you wish to perform a bodily action, you should reflect upon that same bodily action: ‘Would this bodily action that I wish to…
content: “Rāhula, when you wish to perform a bodily action, you should reflect upon that same bodily action: ‘Would this bodily action that I wish to do lead to my own harm, to the harm of others, or to the harm of both? Then this bodily action is unwholesome, leading to suffering, resulting in suffering.’ If, on reflection, you know: ‘This bodily action that I wish to do would lead to my own harm, to the harm of others, or to the harm of both; it is unwholesome, leading to suffering, resulting in suffering’—then such a bodily action you should certainly not do. If, on reflection, you know: ‘This bodily action that I wish to do does not lead to my own harm, nor to the harm of others, nor to the harm of both; it is wholesome, leading to ease, resulting in ease’—then such a bodily action you should do.”

title: “Monks, what is the origination of form? What is the origination of feeling? What is the origination of perception? What is the origination of formations?…
content:
“Monks, what is the origination of form? What is the origination of feeling? What is the origination of perception? What is the origination of formations? What is the origination of consciousness? Here, monks, a monk delights, welcomes, and remains attached. What does he delight in, welcome, and remain attached to? He delights, welcomes, and remains attached to form. Because of his delight, welcome, and attachment to form, delight in form arises. Because of delight in form, clinging to form arises. With clinging to form as condition, becoming arises; with becoming as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering.

He delights, welcomes, and remains attached to feeling … perception … formations … consciousness. Because of his delight, welcome, and attachment to consciousness, delight in consciousness arises. Because of delight in consciousness, clinging to consciousness arises … Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is the origination of form, the origination of feeling, the origination of perception, the origination of formations, the origination of consciousness.”

title: “Greed gives rise to misfortune, Greed stirs up the mind. Greed is the inner fear Born within people. People do not recognize That special kind…
content:
“Greed gives rise to misfortune,
Greed stirs up the mind.
Greed is the inner fear
Born within people.
People do not recognize
That special kind of greed.

The greedy person knows not what is good,
The greedy person sees not the Dhamma.
Blindness and darkness occur
Where greed dwells together.

One who has abandoned greed,
Not greedy for what is to be craved,
For him greed falls away
Like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.

Hatred gives rise to misfortune,
Hatred stirs up the mind.
Hatred is the inner fear
Born within people.
People do not recognize
That special kind of hatred.

The hateful person knows not what is good,
The hateful person sees not the Dhamma.
Blindness and darkness occur
Where hatred dwells together.

One who has abandoned hatred,
Not hating what is hateful,
For him hatred falls away
Like a palm fruit cut from its stalk.

Delusion gives rise to misfortune,
Delusion stirs up the mind.
Delusion is the inner fear
Born within people.
People do not recognize
That special kind of delusion.

The deluded person knows not what is good,
The deluded person sees not the Dhamma.
Blindness and darkness occur
Where delusion dwells together.

One who has abandoned delusion,
Not deluded about what is delusive,
That one dispels all darkness
Like the rising sun.”

title: - “Venerable Sāriputta, what is happiness? What is suffering?” - “Friend, rebirth is suffering; non-rebirth is happiness. When there is rebirth, friend, this suffering is…
content:
- “Venerable Sāriputta, what is happiness? What is suffering?”
- “Friend, rebirth is suffering; non-rebirth is happiness. When there is rebirth, friend, this suffering is to be expected: cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination, contact with fire, contact with a stick, contact with a sword. Even relatives and friends, when they meet and gather together, cause distress. Friend, rebirth is suffering; when there is rebirth, this suffering is to be expected. When there is no rebirth, friend, this happiness is to be expected: no cold, no heat, no hunger, no thirst, no defecation, no urination, no contact with fire, no contact with a stick, no contact with a sword. Even relatives and friends, when they meet and gather together, do not cause distress. Friend, when there is no rebirth, this happiness is to be expected.”

title: “Monks, there are these four noble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging, having known the peril in what is…
content: “Monks, there are these four noble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging, having known the peril in what is subject to aging, seeks the unaging, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to sickness, having known the peril in sickness, seeks the unailing, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to death, having known the peril in death, seeks the deathless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to defilement, having known the peril in defilement, seeks the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. These, monks, are the four noble searches.”

title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that so prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising, or abandons arisen sensual desire, as the sign of…
content: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that so prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising, or abandons arisen sensual desire, as the sign of the foul. The sign of the foul, monks, when wisely attended to, prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising and abandons arisen sensual desire.”

title: Like a great rocky mountain, Standing up to the sky, Advancing and surrounding, Crushing everything on all sides — So too, aging and death Advance…
content:
Like a great rocky mountain,
Standing up to the sky,
Advancing and surrounding,
Crushing everything on all sides —
So too, aging and death
Advance upon beings.
Warriors, brahmins, merchants,
Workers, outcasts,
Those who collect rubbish and feces —
No one can escape.
All are conquered.
No elephant corps,
No chariot corps, no infantry,
No battle of spells,
No battle of wealth
Can help one win
Against aging and death.
Therefore, the wise person,
Seeing what is good for oneself,
Places faith
In the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.
Whoever by body, speech, and mind
Practices in accordance with the Dhamma,
Is praised in this life
And in the next enjoys heavenly bliss.
